title: The naive framing: "my new prompt looks better. Done."
text: A newcomer tweaks their agent's prompt, looks at the new deck, and calls it better. That's a glance, not a measurement. So, what does actually testing a prompt change look like round after round?

title: Stakes: a prompt, edited again, across five tasks
text: You've got a Claude agent that writes slide decks, and you keep editing its system prompt hoping each version beats the last for five different topics every time.

title: The wrong guess: glance in, glance out, ship it
text: The natural read, open the new deck, glance at it next to the old one, and if it looks cleaner, ship it. Glance in, glance out, decision made. Hold on to

title: The anchor: the mandatory-diagram grader
text: One rule, every slide has to carry a real diagram, not just text and boxes, and one grader does nothing but count whether that actually happened. But a

title: Broken, with a case: a font-size floor a glance can't catch
text: Glance won't catch a 9-point caption sitting under the 10-point floor on slide four. A code grader parses the file's actual font sizes and catches it in milliseconds. No eyeballing required. The eval runs in two layers. Layer one

title: Mechanism: layer one, the code checks
text: Is code parsing the deck file itself, slide count, images present, cluttered slides, tiny fonts, stray emoji. No model call, pass or fail in milliseconds.

title: Mechanism: layer two, the LLM judge
text: Layer two hands the rendered slide images to an LLM judge scoring text, imagery, layout, color, and whether the title actually matches the body underneath it. Round one just tightens

title: Mechanism: three rounds, each adding one rule
text: Typography and trims word count. Round two adds that mandatory diagram. Round three adds a QA loop. The agent rasterizes its own deck, inspects every slide for overlap and overflow, fixes what it finds, and checks again before it's done.

title: The anchor returns: the diagram check, empty again
text: Then round four breaks the pattern entirely. It drops every one of those rules and goes back to the plain prompt just on a stronger model. Check that same diagram grader, and it's empty again. That rule only ever lived in the prompt. When a code check fails, no

title: Both directions (A): a code fail, proven at parse time
text: Diagram, a caption under the size floor, that's a concrete defect proven the moment the file's parsed. No judgment call needed. But every code check

title: Both directions (B): all checks pass, judge still needed
text: Passing doesn't mean the deck is good. A slide can hit every rule and still not explain the idea, which is exactly what the LLM judge is there to catch. Score

title: Carry-out
text: Every version against the same fixed test in the same pinned baseline. A rule that only lives in the prompt doesn't survive a model swap. Your turn. Here's

title: Your turn
text: The prompt. Read it with me. Take an agent I'm iterating on. Freeze one fixed test set of real inputs. Write one code check that's just a plain fact present or not and one rubric a judge model can score from the rendered result. Run every version including one where I swap the model instead of the prompt against that same test and the same pinned baseline. What actually moved and what only looked like it moved?
